issues.description: DELETE /admin/users/:id has no authentication or admin authorization middleware, so anyone can delete any user.
The sales report endpoint requires only a logged-in user and has no role check, so any customer can read business-sensitive sales data.

The async login handler has no try/catch and no input validation, and Express 4 does not catch rejected promises, so errors cause unhandled rejections and hung requests; there is also no rate limiting against brute-force attacks.
The async order handler has no error handling or validation of cart/card, so failures leave the request hanging, and raw card data from the request body is passed along (PCI risk).
The client-supplied cart and card are passed to placeOrder without schema validation, which risks malformed input and price or quantity tampering.
Query parameters from/to are passed unvalidated to salesReport (possible injection or invalid dates) and the async handler lacks error handling.
The async delete handler has no error handling, and req.params.id is unvalidated, and a missing user still returns 204.
The Authorization header is passed directly to verifyToken without handling the 'Bearer ' prefix or a missing header, which is fragile and depends on verifyToken's behavior.
The catch block swallows the error without logging, making auth failures hard to diagnose.
The cart-full check runs before looking up an existing SKU, so adding more of an item already in a full cart is rejected even though no new line would be created.
item.quantity is never validated, so negative, zero, fractional, NaN or huge values can reduce the total, produce invalid totals, or bypass limits when added to an existing line.

The whole caller-supplied item is copied into the cart, including priceCents and any extra fields, with no validation or server-side price lookup, which allows price tampering if the data comes from a client.
When a matching SKU exists, a different item.priceCents is silently ignored, so the cart can keep a stale or inconsistent price without any warning.
cartTotal trusts that priceCents and quantity are valid integers, so malformed lines produce NaN, fractional or negative totals, which breaks the integer-cents guarantee.
If connection.query throws, connection.release() on line 12 is never called, leaking the pooled client and eventually exhausting the pool; wrap in try/finally.
Acquiring a dedicated client for every single statement is unnecessary overhead; pool.query(sql, params) handles acquire/release automatically and safely.

Pool is created without error handling, so an idle client error emits an unhandled 'error' event that can crash the process; add pool.on('error', ...) and consider setting max, idleTimeoutMillis, and connectionTimeoutMillis.
No TLS/SSL configuration is specified for the database connection, which may allow unencrypted connections in production unless enforced via the connection string.
query() accepts raw SQL strings with no guard or documentation that callers must use parameterized values, leaving room for SQL injection through string concatenation in other modules.
Check-then-act race condition: stock is read and then updated in separate statements without a transaction or lock, so concurrent reservations can oversell.
The UPDATE query promise is not awaited, so errors become unhandled rejections and the function returns success before the reservation is persisted.
The UPDATE has no guard such as 'AND quantity >= $1', so quantity can go negative if the earlier check is stale; use an atomic conditional update and check affected rows.
The quantity parameter is not validated (negative, zero, non-integer, or NaN values), so a negative quantity would increase stock and bypass the availability check.
Generic Error with an interpolated SKU makes it hard for callers to distinguish insufficient stock programmatically; use a custom error type.
SQL injection: `from` and `to` are concatenated directly into the query string instead of using parameterized queries.
Empty catch block silently swallows database errors, hiding failures and making debugging impossible.
Returning an empty array on error makes a failed query indistinguishable from a period with no sales, producing misleading reports.
No validation of `from`/`to` inputs (type, date format, from <= to) and no authorization check despite being staff-only reporting.
BETWEEN with a date-only `to` value excludes orders created later that day, and GROUP BY alias `day` is not portable across all SQL databases.
orderCount has no error handling, inconsistent with salesReport, and relies on rows[0] existing.
Number() on a COUNT(*) result (often a bigint string) may lose precision for very large counts.
SQL injection: user-supplied email is concatenated directly into the query string instead of using a parameterized query.
MD5 is a fast, broken hash unsuitable for password storage; use bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2 with a per-user salt.
Hash comparison uses non-constant-time `!==`, which may leak timing information; use crypto.timingSafeEqual.
Early return for unknown email skips hashing, creating a timing difference that enables user enumeration.
jwt.sign expiresIn given a bare number is interpreted as seconds, but the config name 'sessionTtlMinutes' implies minutes, so tokens will expire far too soon (or the unit is wrong).
jwt.verify does not restrict allowed algorithms; specify { algorithms: ["HS256"] } to prevent algorithm confusion.
jwt.sign does not specify an algorithm explicitly, relying on library defaults.
No input validation on email/password types or presence; non-string password would cause createHash.update to throw.
user.name is interpolated into HTML without escaping, allowing HTML/content injection (XSS-style) in the email body.
Empty catch block silently swallows send failures, so errors are never logged, retried, or reported to the caller.
Currency is hard-coded to "EUR" rather than using the order's currency, which could show wrong currency to customers.
user.email is used as the recipient without validation or header-injection checks (e.g., newline characters), and the subject is a hard-coded non-localized string.
No input validation for user or order (null/undefined would throw), and no plain-text fallback is provided for the HTML email.
Importing from a stub module (mailer-stub.js) suggests a placeholder mailer is used in production code.
Off-by-one loop condition `i <= cart.items.length` accesses an undefined item on the last iteration, causing a TypeError after all real items are reserved.
Stock is reserved without any rollback if a later reservation or the card charge fails, leaving inventory permanently reserved.
Card is charged with no idempotency key, so retries can double-charge, and there is no refund if the subsequent DB insert fails.
Order insert is not in a transaction with the stock reservation and charge, so failures can leave a charged payment with no order record.
Total is computed from client-supplied cart data without server-side price validation, allowing price tampering.
No validation of userId, cart (empty or malformed items, non-positive quantities), or card input, and no authorization check that the caller owns userId.
Tax is calculated and returned but not included in the charged total or persisted, creating inconsistency between the amount charged and the order data.
Email sending or user lookup failure after the order is charged and saved will throw and make placeOrder appear to fail even though the order succeeded.
Reservations are performed sequentially with await in a loop and there is no error handling or logging around the order flow.
Logs the full card number and CVC in plaintext, which violates PCI DSS and exposes sensitive card data in logs.
chargeCard does not validate card or amountEuros (e.g. NaN, negative, zero, non-number), so invalid or malicious amounts could be sent to the provider.
The provider.charge call has no error handling or idempotency key, so failures propagate unhandled and retries risk duplicate charges.
Math.round(amountEuros * 100) is subject to floating-point errors for some decimal values; amounts should be handled as integer cents or with a decimal library.
Empty catch block silently swallows refund errors, hiding failures and making debugging impossible.
refundCharge returns true even when the refund failed, so callers will believe the customer was refunded when they were not.
refundCharge does not validate chargeId and has no authorization or idempotency checks, allowing arbitrary or repeated refund attempts.
